1	Kennedy Michael (Orcid ID: 0000-0001-5676-2010)
2	
3	- -
4	
5	TITLE:       CANNABIS, CANNABIDIOL AND
6	TETRAHYDROCANNABINOL IN SPORT: AN                                  OVERVIEW
7	
8	
9	AUTHOR:        Michael Kennedy
10	
11	
12	AFFILIATIONS: University of New South Wales (Sydney), Department of Medicine
13	and Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology, St Vincent’s Hospital Darlinghurst.
14	
15	
16	CONTACT AUTHOR EMAIL: drmkenn@ozemail.com.au
17	
18	
19	FUNDING:       None
20	
21	
22	COI:           None
23	
24	
25	ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS: Library services, UNSW
26	
27	
28	CANNABIS, CANNABIDIOL AND TETRAHYDROCANNABINOL IN SPORT:
29	AN OVERVIEW
30	
31	ABSTRACT
32	The World Antidoping Agency now allows cannabidiol (CBD) to be taken
33	in elite sport but has retained all other cannabinoids on its banned list. This,
34	together with liberalisation of cannabis laws have led to an increasing
35	interest in its use in sport. This includes commercial sponsorship of
36	sporting events and highlights the need for accurate information to be
37	readily available to athletes and their advisers. This narrative review
38	confirms that CBD and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) do not enhance
39	performance. CBD possesses anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties
40	which have not been adequately evaluated in the area of sport. Some
41	formulations of CBD contain THC or other cannabinoids that may result
42	in a positive drug test.
43	
44	Relaxation of laws in the United States and elsewhere relating to cannabis
45	have heightened interest in its potential for use in sport and exercise. In
46	2016 Australia the Federal Government legalised access to medicinal
47	cannabis and in December 2020 amended legislation to allow formulations
48	of 98% pure botanical cannabidiol to be placed in Schedule 3 thereby
49	allowing direct consumer purchase from a pharmacy.1.2
50	This article has been accepted for publication and undergone full peer review but has
51	not been through the copyediting, typesetting, pagination and proofreading process
52	which may lead to differences between this version and the Version of Record. Please
53	cite this article as doi: 10.1111/imj.15724
54	                          This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
55	                                       - -
56	
57	Cannabis was one of the many components of the Olympic Victors Dark
58	ointment used in the Ancient Olympics for the relief of pain and swellings.3
59	The present use of cannabis in sport is largely determined by peer contact,
60	information on the internet and other promotional activity.4,5. Numerous
61	high-profile sporting identities in the USA promote cannabis as an adjunct
62	to training, to improve sleep patterns, prevent neurotrauma or relieve
63	musculoskeletal and other discomforts. These include Ross Rebagliti
64	Olympic snow-boarding gold medalist, USA Triatholon partnering with
65	Pure Spectrum CBD and World Surf League appointing cbdMD as official
66	sponsor of the 2019/2020 Jaws Big Wave Championships.6,7 8 Efforts to
67	evaluate its effect on performance and its usefulness as a companion to
68	sport are complicated by variations in doses, formulations, multiple means
69	of drug delivery, user sophistication and multiple active cannabinoids
70	present in the preparations and their complex pharmacology. Literature
71	searches for this narrative review included pub med, medline, Google and
72	a large collection of reprints and proceedings of conferences held by the
73	author.
74	
75	Pharmacology of cannabinoids
76	In addition to the naturally occurring cannabis sativa, indica and ruderalis
77	there are hundreds of cultivated hybrids and large numbers of synthetic
78	analog molecules. Cannabis sativa contains over 66 cannabinoids of which
79	nine belong to the ∆9 group. Cannabis also contains flavinoids and
80	pyrolysis of cannabis produces about 400 products of combustion. Of the
81	cannabinoid acids ∆9 tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), cannabidiol (CBD),
82	cannabichrome and cannabigerol (CBG) are quantitatively the most
83	important. While there is some variation depending on the age of the plant,
84	botanical THC is largely in the inactive form of THC-COOH with
85	pyrolysis releasing the active molecule.9 THC is a partial agonist at central
86	CB1 and peripheral CB2 receptors and is the principal agent causing
87	psychological effects. When inhaled by an experienced user about 10-35%
88	is bioavailable and when taken orally it has a low formulation dependent
89	bioavailability of around 10%. Intravenously THC is largely metabolised
90	by CYP 2C9 and CYP3A4 to predominantly 11—OH THC which has
91	similar psychotropic properties but is present in much lower
92	concentrations. THC concentrations fall rapidly but the terminal t½ ß is up
93	to 57 hours in non-users and shorter half-lives in chronic users.10
94	Cannabidiol is non-psychotropic, has an inhalational bioavailability of
95	31% and terminal t½ of 24-31 hours. It is largely metabolised by CYP 2C19
96	and CYP3A4. Oral bioavailability is also low and formulation dependent.
97	10,11,12
98	         There are many analogs available which have higher binding to CB1
99	receptors with increased psychotropic effects. These are usually
100	                                        - -
101	
102	structurally similar to THC and some have been associated with
103	considerable toxicity. 13
104	
105	Interactions between cannabinoids and exercise
106	Aerobic exercise has a number of effects on the endocannabinoid system.
107	Aerobic exercise results in small elevations in endocannabinoid levels
108	hence a perception that it may be a cause of the “runners high”.14 In regular
109	cannabis users submaximal exercise for 45 minutes results in small
110	elevations of plasma concentrations of THC. These elevations are too small
111	to have a pharmacological effect and are too small to result in
112	misinterpretation of cannabis results detected in drug testing protocols. 15
113	
114	Exercise-induced bronchospasm is inhibited by inhaled THC but not CBD.
115	This is of no therapeutic value in the treatment of asthma due to difficulties
116	in formulation, possible adverse psychological effects and the
117	pharmacodynamic superiority of ß2 agonists as bronchodilator agents. 16,17
118	Aerobic performance and possibly strength is impaired by THC
119	administration. Renaud and Comier found cigarettes with THC 7mg
120	resulted in decreased exercise performance on a bicycle ergometer. 18
121	Steadward and Singh found that 18.2mg THC impaired submaximal
122	performance using a submaximal bicycle protocol.19 A further
123	investigation utilising a modified Masters’ Step Test and increasing oral
124	doses of THC, found 2 out of 12 healthy males were unable to complete
125	the protocol because of dizziness. 20 Strength has been less well assessed
126	after acute administration but decreased strength of finger flexion has been
127	described by Hollister. 21 Four recently published systematic reviews all
128	considered that administered THC does not improve and probably
129	decreases, aerobic exercise and possibly strength. 22,23,24,25 Excluding
130	sportspeople that have had positive drug tests there is only one report of
131	the effect of cannabis in the situation of high-level competition sport this
132	being one small study finding that cannabis impaired performance in mixed
133	martial arts (MMA). 26
134	
135	Chronic cannabis use does not appear to have the same detrimental effect
136	on exercise performance of cannabis users when they are not consuming
137	cannabis at the time. This was first evaluated in 1980 using workers in an
138	industrial setting and quantitated by exercise performance using a bicycle
139	protocol to exhaustion. The participants were either tobacco smokers,
140	marihuana smokers and non-users of either . There was no difference in
141	performance between the three groups. 27 A more recent investigation
142	compared 12 regular users and 12 non-using males aged between 19 and
143	39 recruited from the Colorado University campus. Cardiorespiratory
144	fitness was measured by Bruce Protocol with measurement of VO2 max,
145	                                       - -
146	
147	strength by handgrip, anaerobic power by Wingate protocol, and
148	assessments of lower limb strength by Isokinetic Dynamometer. No
149	significant differences were found between the two groups but there was a
150	tendency for greater fatigue in the marihuana users. 28
151	
152	Almost all exercise and strength investigations have used young subjects
153	<40 years of age. There are none in children. Of more concern are the
154	findings in two earlier investigations on 10 older patients aged 47.3 +/- 6.1
155	and 49.6 +/- 5.9 years with angiographically diagnosed >75% narrowing
156	in at least one coronary artery. Smoking cigarettes containing THC 19.8mg
157	prior to exercise resulted in an earlier onset of angina when compared to
158	both placebo and nicotine containing cigarettes which may be due to the
159	earlier increase in peak double product (heart rate x systolic blood
160	pressure).29,30
161	
162	Use in the general community
163	Cannabis is the most extensively consumed psychoactive drug worldwide.
164	Surveys of the use by sportspeople requires differentiation between use for
165	purely recreational or medicinal consumption and use as an adjunct to
166	sporting activities. With the continuing worldwide liberalisation of laws
167	relating to the use of cannabis presently available figures may be under-
168	estimates of the position in 2022. In the 2016 Australian community
169	cannabis was the most commonly used illicit drug with 10% reporting use
170	in the preceding 12 months. 31
171	
172	Use in top level sport
173	The psychoactive component THC and analogs remain banned substances
174	by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) but CBD is permitted. 32 The
175	urinary concentrations of metabolite THC-COOH detected by WADA
176	accredited laboratories could not be the result of passive exposure and are
177	an indication of use at elite competition level. 33 In a sample covering the
178	period 2014-2017 cannabis constituted around 3% of all positive results
179	the highest use being in weightlifting, wrestling, boxing, cycling,
180	taekwondo, judo and aquatics. 34 In an older survey of 974 elite Australian
181	athletes 3.2% had used cannabis in the past year and 21% had a history of
182	any past use including recreational use. 35 The most recent Australian
183	report of drug testing in the elite did not detect THC in any individual. 36
184	
185	Use in lower-level sport
186	Surveys have been the principal method of determining cannabis use in
187	sportspeople. Sample sizes range from a relatively small number of
188	subjects up to thousands and there is a wide spectrum of results. Published
189	surveys usually comprise of cross-sections of high school and university
190	                                      - -
191	
192	students, sporting organisations, elite athletes, conference attendees and
193	youth surveys. These miss those who are not in organised events or
194	sporting organisations. Almost all respondents are under 40 years old and
195	interpretation of data is complicated by factors such as reluctance to
196	disclose use, details as to the dose and formulation of the active agent(s)
197	used and whether the use relates to some sought after effect in terms of
198	performance or injury. The United States National Health and Nutrition
199	Examination Survey (NHANES) of 20 – 59-year-olds covered the period
200	2007-2014. After excluding 6,441, 12,618 had complete responses to the
201	“Drug use and exercise” section of the questionnaire (never = 5,913, past
202	= 5,109, current = 1,596). The survey concluded that there was lower
203	prevalence of moderate physical activity in users of marihuana than never
204	users, and there were no differences in the levels of exercise between the
205	samples when adjusted for co-variates. 37 A systematic review of 37
206	articles on cannabis use by athletes ranging from amateur school level to
207	elite professionals, found usages ranged from 0.8 - 66.8% lifetime use to
208	2.7 - 62% use in the past year. 24 The studies differed in terms of sport
209	examined, questionnaires used, country and performance level of the
210	participants. One older survey of 1,196 French Sport Science University
211	students found a higher use in those involved in “sliding sports” (wind
212	surfing, skiing, snowboarding, surfing, sailing). 38
213	
214	Social media surveys are now an easy means of accessing target groups of
215	interest. Since cannabis laws have become relaxed some of these results
216	and opinions have been published in peer reviewed literature. The Athlete-
217	Pain Exercise and Cannabis Experience (PEACE) used Facebook and other
218	social media and flyers in sports stores to access triathletes, swimmers,
219	ultra-runners and cyclists. Respondents were largely serious athletes with
220	73% exercising >5 days per week and almost half exercising for >11 hours
221	per week. Of the 1161 who completed the survey 67% had used cannabis
222	and 301 (26%) were current users of which 60% were >40 years old with
223	greater use of CBD in the older athlete. Over half used a cannabis
224	preparation (type unspecified) for sleep, calming down and reducing pain.
225	Other responses cited positive and negative effects on performance,
226	decreasing muscle spasms and anxiety/paranoia and increased energy. 39
227	Another widely advertised online Facebook survey entitled “Cannabis and
228	Health” targeted individuals aged over 21 in states in the USA where
229	cannabis laws had been relaxed. Of the 620 respondents 605 responding to
230	the cannabis questions, with a mean age of 37.5 years old, 81.7% endorsed
231	concurrent use of cannabis (type unspecified) before or after exercise and
232	undertook more exercise than nonusers. The majority of users variously
233	reported it increased enjoyment and improved recovery and motivation to
234	exercise. 37.5% considered it enhanced performance while 62.5%
235	                                      - -
236	
237	disagreed or were neutral on this question. 40 An online survey using two
238	Facebook ultrarunner sites resulted in 609 completed surveys. Of these
239	8.4% of respondents used a performance enhancing agent during training
240	or competition of which cannabis was used in 48%. 41 Ultrarunning is a
241	relatively new sport defined by competing in events of over 50 km and up
242	to >100 miles.
243	
244	In summary, at present, cannabis use by athletes appears to be common,
245	but far from universal. Preparations used usually contain both CBD and
246	THC in various proportions. CBD is considered as an adjunct to training,
247	to improve sleep patterns, prevent neurotrauma or relieve musculoskeletal
248	and other discomforts and its use as a single agent is probably higher in
249	the older age groups. THC is considered , among other reported subjective
250	properties, as being able to improve training by increasing the ability to
251	concentrate on form and as having calming effects and improving appetite.
252	Total cannabis use is probably similar to use in the general community.
253	
254	Adverse effects
255	There is a very extensive literature relating to adverse effects of
256	cannabinoids but there has not been a comprehensive investigation of
257	adverse effects in the area of sport. Data has been gathered only from
258	surveys and occasional case reports. Individuals who have ceased cannabis
259	because of an adverse experience such as a drug related adverse reaction
260	or an accident caused by incoordination are therefore unlikely to be
261	included in most surveys.
262	
263	Excluding illegal sources of street cannabis, at present sportspeople in
264	Australia can administer cannabinoids from pharmaceutically formulated
265	combinations either locally available or imported. Formulations contain
266	THC, CBD and occasionally other botanical cannabinoids in various ratios
267	or as separate agents.       Many use other preparations where the
268	concentrations are not known and contaminants are sometimes likely to be
269	present and co-administered supplements may also be altering the
270	pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the cannabinoids. 42
271	
272	In volunteer studies single doses of THC produce alterations in mood and
273	some of these such as relaxation and disinhibition appear to be considered
274	a positive adjunct to exercise. In one formal exercise investigation one
275	subject became “stoned” and could not continue the exercise protocol after
276	smoking a single cigarette containing THC 20mg. 43
277	
278	Occasionally THC can produce severe paranoia panic attacks and
279	hallucinations. The PEACE investigators reported decreased anxiety,
280	                                        - -
281	
282	calming down effects but also anxiety, paranoia and feelings of uneasiness.
283	39
284	
285	
286	
287	Dose ranging studies of 5, 10, 15 and 20 mg THC administered as capsules
288	cause a dose related decrease in standing steadiness, simple reaction times
289	and visual determination tests lasting up to three hours. 44 These may result
290	in injuries in sports that require high levels of concentration, special
291	awareness and skilled coordination.
292	
293	Cannabinoids have multiple effects on the cardiovascular system. Single
294	inhaled doses of THC cause an increase in heart rate and blood pressure
295	but in a laboratory investigation where doses of THC were increased in a
296	stepwise fashion, 2 of 12 could not complete the protocol because of
297	dizziness related to falls in blood pressure. 20
298	
299	There are a number of case reports of acute cerebrovascular and cardiac
300	events where cannabis is implicated as the causative agent. 45 In the case
301	of patients with coronary disease adverse cardiac effects may occur as the
302	acute elevations of heart rate decrease the threshold for exercise
303	precipitated angina. 29,30 Acute coronary syndromes are rare in the young
304	and in sport but have been attributed to cannabis during sporting activity.
305	46,47
306	
307	
308	
309	Cannabidiol
310	There is considerable interest in and promotion of this non-psychotropic
311	agent as it now allowed in competition sport. Recent narrative reviews on
312	its potential applications in sport have considered possible positive effects
313	in numerous areas such as inflammation, pain, neuroprotection in contact
314	sport, sleep and anxiety and mentioned the lack of and need for, well-
315	designed studies in sport. 48,49 Such studies can be particularly difficult in
316	sportspersons as a recent meta-analysis found athletes have greater pain
317	tolerance than the sedentary. 50
318	
319	There are numerous publications reporting the effects of THC on exercise
320	performance. In contrast there are only three (very recent) publications in
321	the refereed literature that evaluate the effect of CBD administration
322	following either principally upper or lower body exercise.
323	
324	In the first 23 male and female trained weight lifters were divided into 3
325	groups and not crossed over. The effect of CBD on lower body exercise
326	was evaluated by delayed muscle soreness (DOMS) induced by a maximal
327	back squat. DOMS was quantitated by a visual analog scale for up to 96
328	hours post exercise. Immediately post exercise, 8 subjects were
329	                                      - -
330	
331	administered 1 ml of CBD oil 16.67 mg sublingually, 8 subjects were
332	administered 1 ml medium chain triglyceride (MCT) sublingually (SL) and
333	7 subjects (the Null group) did not have any intervention. DOMS scores
334	increased after exercise in all three groups. The CBD group lifted the
335	largest weights (CBD 102.84 + 45.15 kg, MCT 82.39 + 34.44 kg, Null
336	65.91 + 16.23 kg) and had the highest DOMS scores post exercise induced
337	muscle damage (CBD 60.3 + 24.37, MCT 37.99 + 26.94, Null 25.5 +
338	18.34), which fell more rapidly in the CBD group than the MCT and Null
339	groups. The authors concluded there was a greater recovery with CBD but
340	this occurred in the group who lifted considerably heavier weights. 51
341	
342	The second was a double-blind crossover study that required multiple
343	attendances and laboratory investigations and was completed by 16 (14
344	male 2 female) of 21 trained lifters. Strength and power were measured
345	by a maximal back squat and a counter movement maximal jump. Muscle
346	damage was measured by creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin (Myo)
347	levels at 0, 24, 48 and 72 hours. Immediately post exercise a placebo or
348	CBD 60 mg solubilistat was administered, both administered with 250 ml
349	of water. CBD resulted in decreases in the levels of CK and Myo at the
350	p<0.05 level when compared to placebo. There were individual increases
351	and decreases in back squat performance in both groups and no alteration
352	in the countermovement jump. The authors concluded that more data are
353	required for clearer statements in the area. 52
354	
355	The third was a placebo-controlled double-blind crossover study
356	completed by 13 untrained males. An isokinetic dynamometer was used to
357	evaluate muscle power. Muscle damage was measured by use of a visual
358	10-point scale after a series of maximal elbow flexions. Subjects received
359	two doses of 150mg (capsule formulation) or identical placebo containing
360	vegetable oil orally. The first dose was within one hour after exercise and
361	the second 8 hours later. Peak torque measures and the same doses were
362	repeated (a total dose of 300mg daily) at 24, 48 and 72 hours. No
363	differences were found between CBD and placebo in either perceived
364	muscle soreness or power at any time interval. 53
365	
366	No adverse effects due to CBD were reported in the three studies and while
367	the methodologies varied, their combined findings suggest CBD has no
368	substantial positive or negative effect on performance, symptomatic
369	muscle damage or damage parameters.
370	
371	It is very likely CBD would not enhance aerobic performance or strength.
372	Oral doses of 600mg cause slight falls in blood pressure and increases in
373	heart rate in response to hand grip. 54 CBD appears to be free of serious
374	                                        - -
375	
376	adverse effects on a normal cardiovascular system. 55 It does not have the
377	bronchodilator properties of THC. 17
378	
379	The survey of 25 competitive rugby union and league teams in the United
380	Kingdom is probably the largest sport related case series involving a single
381	cannabinoid. Of the 517 players 91% were aware of CBD and 133 had or
382	still used it in various doses and formulations. The commonest reasons for
383	use were recovery from pain (80%) and sleep (78%). Lesser reasons were
384	anxiety (32%) and a small number of “medical reasons” which included
385	recovery from concussion. 4
386	
387	A comprehensive adverse reaction profile for CBD in animals and humans
388	has recently been published. CBD was administered to both children and
389	adults in varying doses of up to 1000mg per day for different periods of
390	time including around 7 weeks in one study of 88 adult patients with
391	treatment resistant psychoses. The incidence of adverse effects reported
392	ranged from 10-93% with a higher incidence being reported in children
393	with refractory epilepsy. The commonest adverse effects were somnolence,
394	sedation, lethargy and gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhoea. Liver
395	function tests may become elevated but it must be remembered that many
396	of the patients were receiving other medications and there is considerable
397	potential for drug interactions with cannabidiol. 56
398	
399	Conclusions
400	In Australia at present cannabis use is probably about the same in sport as
401	it is in the general community though one would expect this to change as
402	promotional activities target this specific market. Formulations of THC and
403	CBD are used in combination or individually with many modes of cannabis
404	delivery. THC and CBD do not appear to be thought of as enhancing
405	performance and surveys of elite sport show their use is well below that of
406	anabolic steroids and stimulants. In relation to adverse effects, anxiety,
407	paranoia palpitations, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, wheezing, coughing
408	and decreased performance have been reported on occasions. Apart from
409	sporadic case reports there are at present few data attributing serious
410	adverse effects to cannabis during sporting activity. Acute cardiovascular
411	events appear rare but have been described with THC.
412	
413	With legalised use in the USA, cannabis is now promoted online and in the
414	general media as an adjunct to sporting activity. In particular, it is promoted
415	to induce calmness and relaxation and decease anxiety and probably to
416	decrease inhibition for more dangerous activities before commencing
417	exercise; to improve focus and concentration during exercise, and to
418	increase feelings of relaxation and relieve musculoskeletal pains and
419	                                       - -
420	
421	muscle stiffness after exercise. None of these parameters, including
422	neuroprotective properties, have been objectively studied in the situation
423	of sport. Older sportspeople and those with known cardiac conditions
424	should be aware of the potential for the development of arrhythmias and
425	acute events. THC and analogs remain banned in elite sport. CBD is
426	allowed but there are virtually no controlled studies of its use in
427	sportspeople. It should be noted that some formulations of CBD may
428	contain sufficient THC to result in a positive test in competition sport. 57
429	In view of the current milieu of cannabinoids, particularly cannabidiol,
430	there is an urgent need for more high quality preclinical and clinical data

TITLE:       CANNABIS, CANNABIDIOL AND
TETRAHYDROCANNABINOL IN SPORT: AN                                  OVERVIEW


AUTHOR:        Michael Kennedy


AFFILIATIONS: University of New South Wales (Sydney), Department of Medicine
and Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology, St Vincent’s Hospital Darlinghurst.


CONTACT AUTHOR EMAIL: drmkenn@ozemail.com.au


FUNDING:       None


COI:           None


ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS: Library services, UNSW


CANNABIS, CANNABIDIOL AND TETRAHYDROCANNABINOL IN SPORT:
AN OVERVIEW

ABSTRACT
The World Antidoping Agency now allows cannabidiol (CBD) to be taken
in elite sport but has retained all other cannabinoids on its banned list. This,
together with liberalisation of cannabis laws have led to an increasing
interest in its use in sport. This includes commercial sponsorship of
sporting events and highlights the need for accurate information to be
readily available to athletes and their advisers. This narrative review
confirms that CBD and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) do not enhance
performance. CBD possesses anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties
which have not been adequately evaluated in the area of sport. Some
formulations of CBD contain THC or other cannabinoids that may result
in a positive drug test.

Relaxation of laws in the United States and elsewhere relating to cannabis
have heightened interest in its potential for use in sport and exercise. In
2016 Australia the Federal Government legalised access to medicinal
cannabis and in December 2020 amended legislation to allow formulations
of 98% pure botanical cannabidiol to be placed in Schedule 3 thereby
allowing direct consumer purchase from a pharmacy.1.2
This article has been accepted for publication and undergone full peer review but has
not been through the copyediting, typesetting, pagination and proofreading process
which may lead to differences between this version and the Version of Record. Please
cite this article as doi: 10.1111/imj.15724
                          This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                       - -

Cannabis was one of the many components of the Olympic Victors Dark
ointment used in the Ancient Olympics for the relief of pain and swellings.3
The present use of cannabis in sport is largely determined by peer contact,
information on the internet and other promotional activity.4,5. Numerous
high-profile sporting identities in the USA promote cannabis as an adjunct
to training, to improve sleep patterns, prevent neurotrauma or relieve
musculoskeletal and other discomforts. These include Ross Rebagliti
Olympic snow-boarding gold medalist, USA Triatholon partnering with
Pure Spectrum CBD and World Surf League appointing cbdMD as official
sponsor of the 2019/2020 Jaws Big Wave Championships.6,7 8 Efforts to
evaluate its effect on performance and its usefulness as a companion to
sport are complicated by variations in doses, formulations, multiple means
of drug delivery, user sophistication and multiple active cannabinoids
present in the preparations and their complex pharmacology. Literature
searches for this narrative review included pub med, medline, Google and
a large collection of reprints and proceedings of conferences held by the
author.

Pharmacology of cannabinoids
In addition to the naturally occurring cannabis sativa, indica and ruderalis
there are hundreds of cultivated hybrids and large numbers of synthetic
analog molecules. Cannabis sativa contains over 66 cannabinoids of which
nine belong to the ∆9 group. Cannabis also contains flavinoids and
pyrolysis of cannabis produces about 400 products of combustion. Of the
cannabinoid acids ∆9 tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), cannabidiol (CBD),
cannabichrome and cannabigerol (CBG) are quantitatively the most
important. While there is some variation depending on the age of the plant,
botanical THC is largely in the inactive form of THC-COOH with
pyrolysis releasing the active molecule.9 THC is a partial agonist at central
CB1 and peripheral CB2 receptors and is the principal agent causing
psychological effects. When inhaled by an experienced user about 10-35%
is bioavailable and when taken orally it has a low formulation dependent
bioavailability of around 10%. Intravenously THC is largely metabolised
by CYP 2C9 and CYP3A4 to predominantly 11—OH THC which has
similar psychotropic properties but is present in much lower
concentrations. THC concentrations fall rapidly but the terminal t½ ß is up
to 57 hours in non-users and shorter half-lives in chronic users.10
Cannabidiol is non-psychotropic, has an inhalational bioavailability of
31% and terminal t½ of 24-31 hours. It is largely metabolised by CYP 2C19
and CYP3A4. Oral bioavailability is also low and formulation dependent.
10,11,12
         There are many analogs available which have higher binding to CB1
receptors with increased psychotropic effects. These are usually
                                        - -

structurally similar to THC and some have been associated with
considerable toxicity. 13

Interactions between cannabinoids and exercise
Aerobic exercise has a number of effects on the endocannabinoid system.
Aerobic exercise results in small elevations in endocannabinoid levels
hence a perception that it may be a cause of the “runners high”.14 In regular
cannabis users submaximal exercise for 45 minutes results in small
elevations of plasma concentrations of THC. These elevations are too small
to have a pharmacological effect and are too small to result in
misinterpretation of cannabis results detected in drug testing protocols. 15

Exercise-induced bronchospasm is inhibited by inhaled THC but not CBD.
This is of no therapeutic value in the treatment of asthma due to difficulties
in formulation, possible adverse psychological effects and the
pharmacodynamic superiority of ß2 agonists as bronchodilator agents. 16,17
Aerobic performance and possibly strength is impaired by THC
administration. Renaud and Comier found cigarettes with THC 7mg
resulted in decreased exercise performance on a bicycle ergometer. 18
Steadward and Singh found that 18.2mg THC impaired submaximal
performance using a submaximal bicycle protocol.19 A further
investigation utilising a modified Masters’ Step Test and increasing oral
doses of THC, found 2 out of 12 healthy males were unable to complete
the protocol because of dizziness. 20 Strength has been less well assessed
after acute administration but decreased strength of finger flexion has been
described by Hollister. 21 Four recently published systematic reviews all
considered that administered THC does not improve and probably
decreases, aerobic exercise and possibly strength. 22,23,24,25 Excluding
sportspeople that have had positive drug tests there is only one report of
the effect of cannabis in the situation of high-level competition sport this
being one small study finding that cannabis impaired performance in mixed
martial arts (MMA). 26

Chronic cannabis use does not appear to have the same detrimental effect
on exercise performance of cannabis users when they are not consuming
cannabis at the time. This was first evaluated in 1980 using workers in an
industrial setting and quantitated by exercise performance using a bicycle
protocol to exhaustion. The participants were either tobacco smokers,
marihuana smokers and non-users of either . There was no difference in
performance between the three groups. 27 A more recent investigation
compared 12 regular users and 12 non-using males aged between 19 and
39 recruited from the Colorado University campus. Cardiorespiratory
fitness was measured by Bruce Protocol with measurement of VO2 max,
                                       - -

strength by handgrip, anaerobic power by Wingate protocol, and
assessments of lower limb strength by Isokinetic Dynamometer. No
significant differences were found between the two groups but there was a
tendency for greater fatigue in the marihuana users. 28

Almost all exercise and strength investigations have used young subjects
<40 years of age. There are none in children. Of more concern are the
findings in two earlier investigations on 10 older patients aged 47.3 +/- 6.1
and 49.6 +/- 5.9 years with angiographically diagnosed >75% narrowing
in at least one coronary artery. Smoking cigarettes containing THC 19.8mg
prior to exercise resulted in an earlier onset of angina when compared to
both placebo and nicotine containing cigarettes which may be due to the
earlier increase in peak double product (heart rate x systolic blood
pressure).29,30

Use in the general community
Cannabis is the most extensively consumed psychoactive drug worldwide.
Surveys of the use by sportspeople requires differentiation between use for
purely recreational or medicinal consumption and use as an adjunct to
sporting activities. With the continuing worldwide liberalisation of laws
relating to the use of cannabis presently available figures may be under-
estimates of the position in 2022. In the 2016 Australian community
cannabis was the most commonly used illicit drug with 10% reporting use
in the preceding 12 months. 31

Use in top level sport
The psychoactive component THC and analogs remain banned substances
by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) but CBD is permitted. 32 The
urinary concentrations of metabolite THC-COOH detected by WADA
accredited laboratories could not be the result of passive exposure and are
an indication of use at elite competition level. 33 In a sample covering the
period 2014-2017 cannabis constituted around 3% of all positive results
the highest use being in weightlifting, wrestling, boxing, cycling,
taekwondo, judo and aquatics. 34 In an older survey of 974 elite Australian
athletes 3.2% had used cannabis in the past year and 21% had a history of
any past use including recreational use. 35 The most recent Australian
report of drug testing in the elite did not detect THC in any individual. 36

Use in lower-level sport
Surveys have been the principal method of determining cannabis use in
sportspeople. Sample sizes range from a relatively small number of
subjects up to thousands and there is a wide spectrum of results. Published
surveys usually comprise of cross-sections of high school and university
                                      - -

students, sporting organisations, elite athletes, conference attendees and
youth surveys. These miss those who are not in organised events or
sporting organisations. Almost all respondents are under 40 years old and
interpretation of data is complicated by factors such as reluctance to
disclose use, details as to the dose and formulation of the active agent(s)
used and whether the use relates to some sought after effect in terms of
performance or injury. The United States National Health and Nutrition
Examination Survey (NHANES) of 20 – 59-year-olds covered the period
2007-2014. After excluding 6,441, 12,618 had complete responses to the
“Drug use and exercise” section of the questionnaire (never = 5,913, past
= 5,109, current = 1,596). The survey concluded that there was lower
prevalence of moderate physical activity in users of marihuana than never
users, and there were no differences in the levels of exercise between the
samples when adjusted for co-variates. 37 A systematic review of 37
articles on cannabis use by athletes ranging from amateur school level to
elite professionals, found usages ranged from 0.8 - 66.8% lifetime use to
2.7 - 62% use in the past year. 24 The studies differed in terms of sport
examined, questionnaires used, country and performance level of the
participants. One older survey of 1,196 French Sport Science University
students found a higher use in those involved in “sliding sports” (wind
surfing, skiing, snowboarding, surfing, sailing). 38

Social media surveys are now an easy means of accessing target groups of
interest. Since cannabis laws have become relaxed some of these results
and opinions have been published in peer reviewed literature. The Athlete-
Pain Exercise and Cannabis Experience (PEACE) used Facebook and other
social media and flyers in sports stores to access triathletes, swimmers,
ultra-runners and cyclists. Respondents were largely serious athletes with
73% exercising >5 days per week and almost half exercising for >11 hours
per week. Of the 1161 who completed the survey 67% had used cannabis
and 301 (26%) were current users of which 60% were >40 years old with
greater use of CBD in the older athlete. Over half used a cannabis
preparation (type unspecified) for sleep, calming down and reducing pain.
Other responses cited positive and negative effects on performance,
decreasing muscle spasms and anxiety/paranoia and increased energy. 39
Another widely advertised online Facebook survey entitled “Cannabis and
Health” targeted individuals aged over 21 in states in the USA where
cannabis laws had been relaxed. Of the 620 respondents 605 responding to
the cannabis questions, with a mean age of 37.5 years old, 81.7% endorsed
concurrent use of cannabis (type unspecified) before or after exercise and
undertook more exercise than nonusers. The majority of users variously
reported it increased enjoyment and improved recovery and motivation to
exercise. 37.5% considered it enhanced performance while 62.5%
                                      - -

disagreed or were neutral on this question. 40 An online survey using two
Facebook ultrarunner sites resulted in 609 completed surveys. Of these
8.4% of respondents used a performance enhancing agent during training
or competition of which cannabis was used in 48%. 41 Ultrarunning is a
relatively new sport defined by competing in events of over 50 km and up
to >100 miles.

In summary, at present, cannabis use by athletes appears to be common,
but far from universal. Preparations used usually contain both CBD and
THC in various proportions. CBD is considered as an adjunct to training,
to improve sleep patterns, prevent neurotrauma or relieve musculoskeletal
and other discomforts and its use as a single agent is probably higher in
the older age groups. THC is considered , among other reported subjective
properties, as being able to improve training by increasing the ability to
concentrate on form and as having calming effects and improving appetite.
Total cannabis use is probably similar to use in the general community.

Adverse effects
There is a very extensive literature relating to adverse effects of
cannabinoids but there has not been a comprehensive investigation of
adverse effects in the area of sport. Data has been gathered only from
surveys and occasional case reports. Individuals who have ceased cannabis
because of an adverse experience such as a drug related adverse reaction
or an accident caused by incoordination are therefore unlikely to be
included in most surveys.

Excluding illegal sources of street cannabis, at present sportspeople in
Australia can administer cannabinoids from pharmaceutically formulated
combinations either locally available or imported. Formulations contain
THC, CBD and occasionally other botanical cannabinoids in various ratios
or as separate agents.       Many use other preparations where the
concentrations are not known and contaminants are sometimes likely to be
present and co-administered supplements may also be altering the
pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the cannabinoids. 42

In volunteer studies single doses of THC produce alterations in mood and
some of these such as relaxation and disinhibition appear to be considered
a positive adjunct to exercise. In one formal exercise investigation one
subject became “stoned” and could not continue the exercise protocol after
smoking a single cigarette containing THC 20mg. 43

Occasionally THC can produce severe paranoia panic attacks and
hallucinations. The PEACE investigators reported decreased anxiety,
                                        - -

calming down effects but also anxiety, paranoia and feelings of uneasiness.
39



Dose ranging studies of 5, 10, 15 and 20 mg THC administered as capsules
cause a dose related decrease in standing steadiness, simple reaction times
and visual determination tests lasting up to three hours. 44 These may result
in injuries in sports that require high levels of concentration, special
awareness and skilled coordination.

Cannabinoids have multiple effects on the cardiovascular system. Single
inhaled doses of THC cause an increase in heart rate and blood pressure
but in a laboratory investigation where doses of THC were increased in a
stepwise fashion, 2 of 12 could not complete the protocol because of
dizziness related to falls in blood pressure. 20

There are a number of case reports of acute cerebrovascular and cardiac
events where cannabis is implicated as the causative agent. 45 In the case
of patients with coronary disease adverse cardiac effects may occur as the
acute elevations of heart rate decrease the threshold for exercise
precipitated angina. 29,30 Acute coronary syndromes are rare in the young
and in sport but have been attributed to cannabis during sporting activity.
46,47



Cannabidiol
There is considerable interest in and promotion of this non-psychotropic
agent as it now allowed in competition sport. Recent narrative reviews on
its potential applications in sport have considered possible positive effects
in numerous areas such as inflammation, pain, neuroprotection in contact
sport, sleep and anxiety and mentioned the lack of and need for, well-
designed studies in sport. 48,49 Such studies can be particularly difficult in
sportspersons as a recent meta-analysis found athletes have greater pain
tolerance than the sedentary. 50

There are numerous publications reporting the effects of THC on exercise
performance. In contrast there are only three (very recent) publications in
the refereed literature that evaluate the effect of CBD administration
following either principally upper or lower body exercise.

In the first 23 male and female trained weight lifters were divided into 3
groups and not crossed over. The effect of CBD on lower body exercise
was evaluated by delayed muscle soreness (DOMS) induced by a maximal
back squat. DOMS was quantitated by a visual analog scale for up to 96
hours post exercise. Immediately post exercise, 8 subjects were
                                      - -

administered 1 ml of CBD oil 16.67 mg sublingually, 8 subjects were
administered 1 ml medium chain triglyceride (MCT) sublingually (SL) and
7 subjects (the Null group) did not have any intervention. DOMS scores
increased after exercise in all three groups. The CBD group lifted the
largest weights (CBD 102.84 + 45.15 kg, MCT 82.39 + 34.44 kg, Null
65.91 + 16.23 kg) and had the highest DOMS scores post exercise induced
muscle damage (CBD 60.3 + 24.37, MCT 37.99 + 26.94, Null 25.5 +
18.34), which fell more rapidly in the CBD group than the MCT and Null
groups. The authors concluded there was a greater recovery with CBD but
this occurred in the group who lifted considerably heavier weights. 51

The second was a double-blind crossover study that required multiple
attendances and laboratory investigations and was completed by 16 (14
male 2 female) of 21 trained lifters. Strength and power were measured
by a maximal back squat and a counter movement maximal jump. Muscle
damage was measured by creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin (Myo)
levels at 0, 24, 48 and 72 hours. Immediately post exercise a placebo or
CBD 60 mg solubilistat was administered, both administered with 250 ml
of water. CBD resulted in decreases in the levels of CK and Myo at the
p<0.05 level when compared to placebo. There were individual increases
and decreases in back squat performance in both groups and no alteration
in the countermovement jump. The authors concluded that more data are
required for clearer statements in the area. 52

The third was a placebo-controlled double-blind crossover study
completed by 13 untrained males. An isokinetic dynamometer was used to
evaluate muscle power. Muscle damage was measured by use of a visual
10-point scale after a series of maximal elbow flexions. Subjects received
two doses of 150mg (capsule formulation) or identical placebo containing
vegetable oil orally. The first dose was within one hour after exercise and
the second 8 hours later. Peak torque measures and the same doses were
repeated (a total dose of 300mg daily) at 24, 48 and 72 hours. No
differences were found between CBD and placebo in either perceived
muscle soreness or power at any time interval. 53

No adverse effects due to CBD were reported in the three studies and while
the methodologies varied, their combined findings suggest CBD has no
substantial positive or negative effect on performance, symptomatic
muscle damage or damage parameters.

It is very likely CBD would not enhance aerobic performance or strength.
Oral doses of 600mg cause slight falls in blood pressure and increases in
heart rate in response to hand grip. 54 CBD appears to be free of serious
                                        - -

adverse effects on a normal cardiovascular system. 55 It does not have the
bronchodilator properties of THC. 17

The survey of 25 competitive rugby union and league teams in the United
Kingdom is probably the largest sport related case series involving a single
cannabinoid. Of the 517 players 91% were aware of CBD and 133 had or
still used it in various doses and formulations. The commonest reasons for
use were recovery from pain (80%) and sleep (78%). Lesser reasons were
anxiety (32%) and a small number of “medical reasons” which included
recovery from concussion. 4

A comprehensive adverse reaction profile for CBD in animals and humans
has recently been published. CBD was administered to both children and
adults in varying doses of up to 1000mg per day for different periods of
time including around 7 weeks in one study of 88 adult patients with
treatment resistant psychoses. The incidence of adverse effects reported
ranged from 10-93% with a higher incidence being reported in children
with refractory epilepsy. The commonest adverse effects were somnolence,
sedation, lethargy and gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhoea. Liver
function tests may become elevated but it must be remembered that many
of the patients were receiving other medications and there is considerable
potential for drug interactions with cannabidiol. 56

Conclusions
In Australia at present cannabis use is probably about the same in sport as
it is in the general community though one would expect this to change as
promotional activities target this specific market. Formulations of THC and
CBD are used in combination or individually with many modes of cannabis
delivery. THC and CBD do not appear to be thought of as enhancing
performance and surveys of elite sport show their use is well below that of
anabolic steroids and stimulants. In relation to adverse effects, anxiety,
paranoia palpitations, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, wheezing, coughing
and decreased performance have been reported on occasions. Apart from
sporadic case reports there are at present few data attributing serious
adverse effects to cannabis during sporting activity. Acute cardiovascular
events appear rare but have been described with THC.

With legalised use in the USA, cannabis is now promoted online and in the
general media as an adjunct to sporting activity. In particular, it is promoted
to induce calmness and relaxation and decease anxiety and probably to
decrease inhibition for more dangerous activities before commencing
exercise; to improve focus and concentration during exercise, and to
increase feelings of relaxation and relieve musculoskeletal pains and
                                       - -

muscle stiffness after exercise. None of these parameters, including
neuroprotective properties, have been objectively studied in the situation
of sport. Older sportspeople and those with known cardiac conditions
should be aware of the potential for the development of arrhythmias and
acute events. THC and analogs remain banned in elite sport. CBD is
allowed but there are virtually no controlled studies of its use in
sportspeople. It should be noted that some formulations of CBD may
contain sufficient THC to result in a positive test in competition sport. 57
In view of the current milieu of cannabinoids, particularly cannabidiol,
there is an urgent need for more high quality preclinical and clinical data
to improve our understanding in this area.

                                                                                                                                              Considerations for Velocity-Based Training: The
                                                                                                                                              Instruction to Move “As Fast As Possible” Is Less
                                                                                                                                              Effective Than a Target Velocity
                                                                                                                                              Steven M. Hirsch and David M. Frost
                                                                                                                                              Faculty of Kinesiology and Physical Education, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada



                                                                                                                                                Abstract
                                                                                                                                                Hirsch, SM and Frost, DM. Considerations for velocity-based training: the instruction to move “as fast as possible” is less effective
                                                                                                                                                than a target velocity. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000–000, 2019—In addition to the potential benefits with monitoring training
                                                                                                                                                intensity with velocity-measuring tools during exercise, these devices also provide an opportunity for researchers and practitioners




Downloaded from http://journals.lww.com/nsca-jscr by BhDMf5ePHKbH4TTImqenVABVvpFq8GojVtTGEE8I2difL0nBqPB4J688mlAd5p2W on 03/18/2020
                                                                                                                                                to provide feedback and instruction to performers in a new way. The purpose of this study was to assess the influence of instructing
                                                                                                                                                athletes with a target velocity vs. instructing them to move “as fast as possible” during a free-weight bench press. In addition, the
                                                                                                                                                effects of each instruction on future repetition maximum (RM) test performance was compared. Thirteen male powerlifters were
                                                                                                                                                recruited and performed 4 sets of 5 repetitions with 45% 1RM while being instructed to attain a target velocity of 1.0 m·s21 or to
                                                                                                                                                move as fast as possible. The maximum mean velocity attained in each set was compared with a repeated measures analysis of
                                                                                                                                                variance and Tukey’s post-hoc test. After these 4 sets of 5 repetitions, the number of repetitions performed during an RM test with
                                                                                                                                                75% 1RM was compared with a Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test. Participants moved faster when they received the target velocity
                                                                                                                                                instruction (0.84 6 0.10 m·s21) than when they received the “move as fast as possible” instruction (0.82 6 0.09 m·s21) (p , 0.001)
                                                                                                                                                with no differences in the number of repetitions performed in the following RM test between the 2 testing sessions (p 5 0.43). An
                                                                                                                                                instruction to attain a challenging velocity target may be a more effective strategy to use when attempting to elicit maximum barbell
                                                                                                                                                velocities during training relative to the traditional instruction to move as fast as possible.
                                                                                                                                                Key Words: speed, power, feedback, bench press, exercise

                                                                                                              training: Insights from a survey of allied health practitioners. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000–000, 2023—This study investigated the

                                                                                                              preventing some practitioners from prescribing BFR. An online survey was disseminated globally to allied health practitioners, with data
                                                                                                              from 397 responders included in analyses. Responders who had prescribed BFR exercise (n 5 308) completed questions about how
                                                                                                              they implement this technique. Those who had not prescribed BFR exercise (n 5 89) provided information on barriers to using this
                                                                                                              technique, and a subset of these responders (n 5 22) completed a follow-up survey to investigate how these barriers could be
                                                                                                              alleviated. Most practitioners prescribe BFR exercise for musculoskeletal rehabilitation clients (91.6%), with the BFR cuff pressure
                                                                                                              typically relative to arterial occlusion pressure (81.1%) and implemented with resistance (96.8%) or aerobic exercise (42.9%). Most
                                                                                                              practitioners screen for contraindications (68.2%), although minor side effects, including muscle soreness (65.8%), are common. The
                                                                                                              main barriers preventing some practitioners from using BFR are lack of equipment (60.2%), insufficient education (55.7%), and safety
                                                                                                              concerns (31.8%). Suggestions to alleviate these barriers included developing educational resources about the safe application and
                                                                                                              benefits of BFR exercise (n 5 20) that are affordable (n 5 3) and convenient (n 5 4). These results indicate that BFR prescription for
                                                                                                              clinical and older cohorts mainly conforms with current guidelines, which is important considering the potentially increased risk for
                                                                                                              adverse events in these cohorts. However, barriers still prevent broader utility of BFR training, although some may be alleviated through

 "domains":["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],

 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Randomised comparison of four 8-week velocity-based back squat programmes (linear, undulating, reverse and constant) in 43 young, moderately strength-trained men (physically active sport science students, 1.5 to 4 years of resistance training experience) who trained twice a week. All four groups increased 1RM squat, squat velocity, countermovement jump height and 20 m sprint performance within the group (for example, 1RM gains of 10.9% to 18.0%), but the authors report no significant group by time interactions for any outcome.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The sample was young, moderately strength-trained men who were physically active sport science students, not described as competitive athletes, and the study used a Smith machine and only two sessions a week. The four groups differed in training intensity and loading patterns, so the study shows no difference between models rather than a ranking of them.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the within-group gains as proof that a given velocity-based programme works, when the study found no significant between-model differences and had no untrained control group.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Riscart-López J, Rendeiro-Pinho G, Mil-Homens P, Soares-daCosta R, Loturco I, Pareja-Blanco F, et al. Effects of four different velocity-based training programming models on strength gains and physical performance. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2020. [Volume, issue and pages not printed in extracted text.]",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000003934",
   "abstract":"Forty-three moderately strength-trained men were randomly assigned to linear, undulating, reverse or constant velocity-based training models and followed an 8-week full squat programme. All groups trained at similar average relative intensity, velocity loss, number of sets and rest. All groups improved 1RM, velocity-related outcomes, countermovement jump and 20 m sprint time, with no significant group by time interactions.",
   "tldr":"Four different velocity-based squat programming models, matched for average intensity, velocity loss, sets and rest, produced similar gains in squat strength, jump height and sprint time in moderately trained men over 8 weeks. The time course of strength gains looked less pronounced in the undulating group, but that difference was not statistically significant.",
   "methods":"Forty-six men were recruited and 43 completed an 8-week intervention of two sessions per week. Groups (linear n=11, undulating n=10, reverse n=11, constant n=11) differed only in programming model. Velocity was measured for every repetition with a linear velocity transducer, and loads were adjusted to the velocity-predicted %1RM. Pre- and post-tests included predicted 1RM, velocity at common loads, countermovement jump and 20 m sprint time. Analysis used a 4 x 2 ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests.",
   "findings":"No significant group by time interactions were found for 1RM, velocity variables, countermovement jump or sprint time. Within groups, 1RM rose significantly in all four groups (about 11% in the undulating group to 18% in the reverse group). Countermovement jump height and sprint time also improved within groups, with effect sizes of about 0.3 to 0.5 for jump height and 0.3 for sprint time. The constant group trained with a significantly slower average velocity than the other groups.",
   "limitations":"Smith machine used for testing and training, which limits transfer to free-weight training. Sample was moderately trained recreational men (not elite athletes) and training frequency was two sessions a week. Between-group differences were not significant, and the undulating group's slower time course in 1RM was described as a non-significant trend. The PDF prints 2020 as the publication year, while the Crossref record gives 2021; the PDF year is used here.",
   "practicalImplications":"In moderately trained men, a velocity-based squat programme using 20% velocity loss within sets, 3 sets and 4 minutes of rest produced similar strength and jump gains whichever loading model was used. Coaches can choose among these models for variety, but the undulating model showed a non-significant trend toward smaller strength gains over the 8 weeks, which matters if strength gain is the priority.",
   "athleteDev":"Velocity-based squat programming with monitored velocity loss can be used to build strength and jump performance in moderately trained adults. The four programming models gave similar results, so selection can rest on the coach's preference or the timing of the training block.",
   "rtp":"The study did not include injured people or a return-to-sport outcome. It cannot be used to set loads or progressions during rehabilitation or to judge readiness to return to play."
 }
}

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Abstract
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Riscart-López, J, Rendeiro-Pinho, G, Mil-Homens, P, Costa, RS-d, Loturco, I, Pareja-Blanco, F, and León-Prados, JA. Effects of
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Four different velocity-based training programming models on strength gains and physical performance. J Strength Cond Res
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              XX(X): 000–000, 2020—The aim of this study was to compare the effects of 4 velocity-based training (VBT) programming models
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              (linear programming [LP], undulating programming [UP], reverse programming [RP], and constant programming [CP]) on the
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              physical performance of moderately strength-trained men. Forty-three young (age: 22.9 6 4.8 years; body mass [BM]: 71.7 6 7.6;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              full squat [SQ] relative strength 1.32 6 0.29) subjects were randomly assigned to LP (gradually increase training intensity and
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              decrease volume), UP (volume and intensity increase or decrease repeatedly), RP (gradually increases volume and decrease
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              intensity), and CP (maintains constant volume and intensity) groups and followed an 8-week VBT intervention using the SQ exercise
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              and monitoring movement velocity for every repetition. All groups trained with similar relative average intensity (67.5% 1 repetition
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              maximum [1RM]), magnitude of velocity loss within the set (20%), number of sets (3), and interset recoveries (4 minutes) throughout
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              the training program. Pre-training and post-training measurements included predicted SQ (1RM), average velocity attained for all
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              loads common to pre-tests and post-tests (AV), average velocity for those loads that were moved faster (AV . 1) and slower (AV ,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              1) than 1 m·s21 at pre-tests, countermovement jump height (CMJ), and 20-m sprint time (T20). No significant group 3 time
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              interactions were observed for any of the variables analyzed. All groups obtained similar increases (shown in effect size values) in
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              1RM strength (LP: 0.88; UP: 0.54; RP: 0.62; CP: 0.51), velocity-load-related variables (LP: 0.74–4.15; UP: 0.46–5.04; RP:
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              0.36–3.71; CP: 0.74–3.23), CMJ height (LP: 0.35; UP: 0.53; RP: 0.49; CP: 0.34), and sprint performance (LP: 0.34; UP: 0.35; RP:
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              0.32; CP: 0.30). These results suggest that different VBT programming models induced similar physical performance gains in
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              moderately strength-trained subjects.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Key Words: strength training, dose-response, athletic performance, training periodization, training prescription, velocity loss

 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Athlete Wellbeing","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Sports Medicine"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Male Athletes","Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Randomly assigned controlled trial of 25 elite athletes from 12 individual and combined sports (12 in the intervention group, 13 in the control group) over 2 weeks. The intervention group turned off devices 30 minutes before bed and had 20 minutes of morning bright light (about 10,000 lux). Within the intervention group, POMS vigor, reaction time, rebound jump height and rebound jump index improved, with significant group by day interactions for these measures, while actigraphy sleep measures did not change. Epworth sleepiness and squat jump interactions were not significant (p=0.095 and p=0.085).",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only 25 athletes were analysed after 13 of the 38 randomised were excluded, leaving 12 and 13 per group, and the author reports a post hoc power of 0.68. The intervention group had lower baseline rebound jump height and index than controls, no blinding is described, and training could not be controlled.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read this as proof that screen restriction and morning light improve athletes' sleep or performance, when measured sleep did not change and most performance gains rest on a few outcomes with small, underpowered comparisons.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Hoshikawa M. Effects of nightly electronic device restriction and morning bright light on sleep, mood, and performance among elite athletes. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025;39(11):1155-1162.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000005201",
   "abstract":"Twenty-five elite athletes were divided into an intervention group (n=12), who turned off electronic devices 30 minutes before bed and had 20 minutes of morning bright light (about 10,000 lux), and a control group (n=13). Sleep, sleepiness, mood and performance were monitored over 2 weeks. The intervention group improved POMS vigor, reaction time, rebound jump height and rebound jump index without a change in sleep parameters. Epworth sleepiness and squat jump changes were not significant between groups.",
   "tldr":"Two weeks of stopping device use 30 minutes before bed and 20 minutes of morning bright light improved mood, reaction time and rebound jump performance in elite athletes. Sleep did not change, and several between-group comparisons were borderline in a small sample.",
   "methods":"Randomised controlled trial in 25 elite athletes (11 men, 14 women) from 12 sports, allocated to intervention (n=12) or control (n=13), after 13 of 38 initially randomised athletes were excluded. Over 2 weeks, actigraphy, Karolinska sleepiness, subjective sleep quality, fatigue and morning heart rate were recorded daily. Before and after the period, Epworth sleepiness, POMS, psychomotor vigilance reaction time, grip strength, squat and rebound jumps, and heart rate during 5 minutes of cycling were measured. Analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests.",
   "findings":"Within the intervention group, POMS vigor rose from 14.6 to 25.9 (p<0.001), reaction time fell from 240 to 225 ms (p=0.001), rebound jump height rose from 28.6 to 30.6 cm (p<0.001) and rebound jump index rose from 1.56 to 1.73 (p<0.001). Group by day interactions were significant for POMS vigor (p=0.042), reaction time (p=0.032), rebound jump height (p=0.031) and rebound jump index (p=0.017). Epworth sleepiness fell in both groups, and the interaction was not significant (p=0.095). Squat jump height rose in the intervention group (30.7 to 33.2 cm, p=0.016), with a non-significant interaction (p=0.085). Grip strength and exercise heart rate showed no significant interaction. Actigraphy sleep measures did not change in either group.",
   "limitations":"Small sample and post hoc power of 0.68, so type II error is likely. Thirteen athletes were excluded after random assignment, leaving unequal groups. The intervention group had lower baseline rebound jump height and index than controls (between-group p<0.05 to 0.01). Training could not be controlled, and self-reported sleep and mood data were collected in a non-blinded design. The author notes that athletes had irregular sleep schedules, which may limit generalisation. The intervention did not change sleep, so mechanism remains unclear. The PDF prints 2025, matching the Crossref year.",
   "practicalImplications":"In elite athletes with irregular sleep schedules, a short two-week routine of stopping device use 30 minutes before bed and 20 minutes of morning bright light was associated with better mood, faster reaction times and better rebound jump performance. Staff should not expect it to change measured sleep, and objective sleep tracking is more reliable than self-report for judging sleep habits.",
   "athleteDev":"The protocol can be considered as a low-burden way to support alertness and mood before training, with reaction time and rebound jump as the outcomes to track. The effects were not consistent across all measures, and because sleep did not change, the benefit should not be described as better sleep.",
   "rtp":"The athletes were not injured and return to sport was not assessed. The study cannot be used to decide readiness to return to play or to guide rehabilitation timelines."
 }

   "methods":"Randomised controlled trial in 25 elite athletes (11 men, 14 women) from 12 sports, allocated to intervention (n=12) or control (n=13), after 13 of 38 initially randomised athletes were excluded. Over 2 weeks, actigraphy, Karolinska sleepiness, subjective sleep quality, fatigue and morning heart rate were recorded daily. Before and after the period, Epworth sleepiness, POMS, psychomotor vigilance reaction time, grip strength, squat and rebound jumps, and heart rate during 5 minutes of cycling were measured. Analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests.",

Group by day interactions were significant for POMS vigor (p=0.042), reaction time (p=0.032), rebound jump height (p=0.031) and rebound jump index (p=0.017).
