Original Research



      Effects of Nightly Electronic Device Restriction and
      Morning Bright Light on Sleep, Mood, and
      Performance Among Elite Athletes
      Masako Hoshikawa
      Department of Sport Science and Research, Japan Institute of Sports Sciences, Kita, Tokyo, Japan



        Abstract
        Hoshikawa, M. Effects of nightly electronic device restriction and morning bright light on sleep, mood, and performance among elite
        athletes. J Strength Cond Res 39(11): 1155–1162, 2025—This study aimed to evaluate whether restriction of electronic device use
        before bedtime and morning bright-light exposure influences sleep, sleepiness, mood, and performance parameters among elite
        athletes. Twenty-five elite athletes (24 international level and 1 national level) were divided into 2 groups: with (INT; n 5 12) and
        without (CON; n 5 13) intervention. The INT turned off their electronic devices 30 minutes before bedtime and were exposed to
        morning bright light (approximately 10,000 lux) for 20 minutes after waking. Their nocturnal sleep parameters, Karolinska sleepiness
        scale, subjective sleep quality, fatigue, and heart rate immediately after waking were monitored every morning for 2 weeks. The
        Epworth sleepiness scale (ESS) score, Profile of Mood States (POMS) vigor and fatigue scores, reaction time, isometric grip
        strength, squat jump (SJ) height, rebound jump (RJ) height, RJ index, and heart rate during aerobic exercise were evaluated before
        and after the 2-week period. The RJ index was calculated as RJ height (m)/ground contact time (sec). For the INT, POMS vigor score
        (p , 0.001), reaction time (p 5 0.016), RJ height (p 5 0.001), and RJ index (p , 0.001) improved without any change in sleep
        parameters. The improvements in ESS score and SJ height seemed to be greater in the INT group, but the interactions did not reach
        a significant level (p , 0.10). No statistically significant interaction was observed in the exercise heart rate and isometric grip
        strength. Two weeks of 30 minutes nighttime electronic device restriction and 20 minutes morning bright-light exposure improved
        mood and some performance parameters among elite athletes. However, the intervention did not change athletes’ sleep
        parameters.

 "confidence":"high",

 "audiences":["Rehabilitation","Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Injured Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of six randomised controlled trials (205 competitive and recreational athletes, mean age 24 years) comparing photobiomodulation with placebo, aloe gel or standard physical therapy for injury-related pain. Pooled pain reduction favoured photobiomodulation (SMD 1.03, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.63, p=0.0089, I2 46.9%), while the two trials that measured return to play were summarised narratively and did not show a benefit.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only five or six small trials were pooled, against a mix of placebo, aloe gel and standard physical therapy comparators, with moderate heterogeneity. The two return-to-play trials used different designs and could not be pooled. The protocol was not prospectively registered, and injury severity was not reported in the included studies.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the pooled pain effect as evidence that photobiomodulation shortens return to play, when the two trials that measured return to play did not show a benefit.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Morgan RM, Wheeler TD, Poolman MA, Haugen ENJ, LeMire SD, Fitzgerald JS. Effects of photobiomodulation on pain and return to play of injured athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(6):e310-e319.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000004752",
   "abstract":"This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated photobiomodulation (PBM) for musculoskeletal pain and time to return to play in injured athletes. Six randomised controlled trials, including 205 competitive and recreational athletes with a mean age of 24 years, were included. PBM reduced pain compared with control groups (SMD 1.03, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.63, p=0.0089). The two trials on time to return to play did not support a benefit of PBM.",
   "tldr":"In injured athletes, photobiomodulation reduced pain more than control treatments across six small randomised trials. The two trials that measured return to play did not show a benefit, so the pain result should not be read as proof that PBM speeds return to play.",
   "methods":"Systematic search of MEDLINE Complete, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, PubMed, Web of Science and Embase, with secondary searches to 7 November 2023, supplemented by reference lists and Google Scholar. Included studies were English-language peer-reviewed randomised controlled trials in athletes aged 18 to 44 years reporting pain or return to play after injury. Two reviewers screened independently, with a third resolving disagreements. Quality was rated with the PEDro scale (Cohen's kappa 1). Pain effects were pooled with a random-effects model in Meta-Essentials, and return-to-play data were summarised narratively.",
   "findings":"Six trials were included, published between 2004 and 2022, with PEDro scores of 6 to 10. The pooled pain effect favoured photobiomodulation over control groups (SMD 1.03, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.63, p=0.0089, I2 46.9%). Of the two return-to-play trials, one found a shorter return with aloe gel than with photobiomodulation (about 8 vs 11 days), and the other found no difference between photobiomodulation and placebo (about 23 to 24 days in each group).",
   "limitations":"The meta-analysis of pain included only five trials according to the Discussion, while the Abstract and Results state six trials, so the number pooled is inconsistent. Return-to-play data could not be pooled, and the aloe gel and placebo comparators differ from one another. Heterogeneity was moderate. The protocol was not registered, and the authors note that the review was part of a broader performance project. Injury severity was not reported in the trials, and small samples limit precision.",
   "practicalImplications":"Clinicians working with injured athletes may use photobiomodulation as an adjunct to reduce pain, using devices with wavelengths between 810 and 980 nm as in the included trials. The authors suggest 3 to 10 minutes per application, 3 to 4 times per week, for at least 3 to 8 weeks. It should not be expected to shorten time to return to play.",
   "athleteDev":"This review does not assess performance outcomes in healthy athletes, so it does not support photobiomodulation as a way to improve training or competition performance. Its findings apply to pain management in injured athletes.",
   "rtp":"The pain findings can inform symptom management during rehabilitation. The two return-to-play trials, with different comparators and no pooled estimate, showed no clear benefit, so the review cannot be used to set or shorten return-to-play timelines."
 }
}

                                                                                                              Abstract
                                                                                                              Morgan, RM, Wheeler, TD, Poolman, MA, Haugen, ENJ, LeMire, SD, and Fitzgerald, JS. Effects of photobiomodulation on pain and
                                                                                                              return to play of injured athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 38(6): e310–e319, 2024—The aims
                                                                                                              of this systematic review and meta-analysis were to evaluate the effect of photobiomodulation (PBM) on musculoskeletal pain in
                                                                                                              injured athletes and to determine if the effects of PBM allowed injured athletes to return to play faster. Electronic databases
                                                                                                              (MEDLINE Complete, CINAHL, and SPORTDiscus, PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase) were systematically searched (up to
                                                                                                              and including November 7, 2023) for peer-reviewed randomized controlled trials (RCTs) meeting criteria. Six RCTs, representing
                                                                                                              205 competitive and recreational athletes with a mean age of 24 years, were included in the analysis. There were 6 intervention
                                                                                                              groups using standard physical therapy (n 5 1), placebo PBM (n 5 4), and aloe gel (n 5 1) lasting between 10 minutes and 8 weeks
                                                                                                              in duration. The level of significance set for the study was p , 0.05. Overall, the use of PBM indicated a positive effect on pain
                                                                                                              reduction for PBM vs. control groups, standardized mean differences 5 1.03, SE 5 0.22, 95% confidence intervals 5 [0.43–1.63],
                                                                                                              p 5 0.0089, but the 2 RCTs found evaluating the effect of PBM on time to return to play after injury in athletes do not support
                                                                                                              a benefit. Allied healthcare professionals may use PBM to reduce pain, thus allowing an athlete to return to their normal bio-

                                                                                                              mechanical movement faster; however, limited evidence suggests that PBM does not reduce time to return to play after an injury.

It summarises ACSM guidance, US and French military recurrence data, and Israel Defense Force heat tolerance test (HTT) data, in which 6 of 145 soldiers tested after a prior heat stroke had a recurrent heat illness, with a reported sensitivity of 66.7% and specificity of 77.7%.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No systematic search or appraisal is described, so the review is selective and reflects the authors' views. The article states that the data are insufficient to support HTT as a diagnostic test.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the heat tolerance test as a validated clearance tool for athletes, when the authors say its data are insufficient for diagnosis and it was developed for young soldiers.",
 "paper": {

  "citation": "O'Connor FG, Heled Y, Deuster PA. Exertional heat stroke, the return to play decision, and the role of heat tolerance testing: a clinician's dilemma. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2018;17(7):244-248.",
  "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000000502",
  "abstract": "Exertional heat stroke is a leading preventable cause of morbidity and mortality in athletes and warfighters. Because a prior event is an important risk factor, return to play or duty decisions after heat stroke are difficult. This special communication reviews current guidance and evidence on these decisions and the potential role of heat tolerance testing, which exposes a person to a controlled heat load to assess heat tolerance.",
  "tldr": "Return to play after exertional heat stroke has no evidence-based guideline. The authors suggest combining history, clinical biomarkers and, where indicated, a heat tolerance test, which has useful but limited diagnostic data.",
  "methods": "Special communication. A clinical case is used to frame the problem. The authors review ACSM return-to-play recommendations, US and French military recurrence studies, and the Israel Defense Force heat tolerance test protocol and results. No systematic search is described.",
  "findings": "The article describes ACSM guidance of at least 7 days without exercise after release, follow-up laboratory tests at about 1 week, a gradual 2-week return in a cool environment, and a laboratory heat tolerance test if vigorous activity is not reached within 4 weeks. In an IDF study, 6 of 145 soldiers who had a heat tolerance test after prior heat stroke had recurrent heat illness; 4 of 35 classified as heat intolerant and 2 of 110 classified as heat tolerant had recurrence. Reported sensitivity, specificity and accuracy were 66.7%, 77.7% and 77.2%. The test protocol uses a 120-minute treadmill walk at 40 degrees C, with heat intolerance defined by rectal temperature above 38.5 degrees C, heart rate above 150 bpm, or no plateau.",
  "limitations": "Selective narrative with no systematic search or quality appraisal, and the authors state their conclusions are a collective opinion. The HTT criteria come from young, moderately fit soldiers and are not adjusted for sex, aerobic capacity, training, acclimatisation or body fat. The reported recurrence data come from a single military population. The article states that HTT is not yet supported as a diagnostic test. The PDF prints 2018, matching Crossref.",
  "practicalImplications": "After exertional heat stroke, return to activity should be gradual over about 2 weeks in a cool environment, with follow-up laboratory tests and a clinical check. Clinicians should use history, biomarkers and functional observations together, and consider a laboratory heat tolerance test if the athlete has not returned to vigorous activity within 4 weeks. Heat tolerance test results should be interpreted with the test's population and adjustment limits in mind.",
  "athleteDev": "Heat tolerance testing is a laboratory test in a controlled chamber and is not a performance measure. Its results are shaped by fitness and acclimatisation, which the protocol does not adjust for, so training staff should not use it to rank athletes' heat tolerance.",
  "rtp": "This article is directly about return-to-play decisions after exertional heat stroke. It supports gradual reintroduction with follow-up testing and a heat tolerance test when recovery stalls, but it states that no evidence-based guideline exists and that the test cannot yet be relied on as a diagnostic or clearance tool."

 "evidenceSummary": "Single-author narrative review of cannabis, cannabidiol (CBD) and THC use in sport.  "screeningLimitations": "The literature search was not systematic (PubMed, Medline, Google and the author's own reprints), so selection of studies is open to bias.  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the CBD recovery results as proof that CBD speeds recovery in athletes, when the author concludes the three trials showed no substantial effect: the faster DOMS recovery came from a group that lifted heavier loads, and the lower CK and myoglobin in a second trial came with no change in performance.",
 "paper": {

  "abstract": "This narrative review states that the World Anti-Doping Agency permits CBD in competition but still bans THC and other cannabinoids.   "tldr": "Cannabis use by athletes appears common but not universal, and the review finds no good evidence that CBD or THC improves performance. THC impaired aerobic performance in the studies cited, and the three small CBD trials in trained lifters and untrained men showed no clear benefit for muscle soreness or strength.",
  "methods": "Narrative review. Literature was identified through PubMed, Medline, Google and the author's reprint collection. No systematic search or formal quality appraisal is described.",
  "findings": "Acute THC reduced aerobic performance and possibly strength in the studies cited.   "limitations": "The review is non-systematic and the author states that controlled data on CBD in athletes are very limited.   "practicalImplications": "Staff should assume that THC is banned in competition and that some CBD products may contain enough THC to produce a positive test. {
 "id": "Q10",
 "sourceFile": "Considerations for Velocity Based Training - The instruction to move as fast as possible is less effective than a target velocity .pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Considerations for Velocity-Based Training: The Instruction to Move As Fast As Possible Is Less Effective Than a Target Velocity' by Hirsch and Frost matches the filename and the Crossref title for externalDoi 10.1519/jsc.0000000000003233.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Within-subject crossover study of 13 male powerlifters (mean age 26.8 years, at least one sanctioned competition) who completed two sessions in randomised order. In each session they performed 4 sets of 5 bench press repetitions at 45% 1RM, instructed either to reach a target mean velocity of 1.0 m/s or to move as fast as possible. The fastest repetition velocity in each set was higher with the target instruction (0.84 vs 0.82 m/s, p=0.0002), and the number of repetitions completed in a subsequent 75% 1RM set did not differ (9.6 vs 10.0, p=0.43).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 13 powerlifters were analysed, on one exercise and one load, with both conditions given feedback after each repetition. The outcome was the fastest repetition of each set, and the authors note that an average of all repetitions might have shown no difference. The 1.0 m/s target was fixed rather than individualised, and only one participant reached it.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 0.02 m/s difference in best-repetition velocity as evidence that target velocity improves training adaptations or strength, when the study measured only same-session velocity and one repetition test.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2019,
  "citation": "Hirsch SM, Frost DM. Considerations for velocity-based training: the instruction to move \"as fast as possible\" is less effective than a target velocity. J Strength Cond Res. 2019.",
  "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000003233",
  "abstract": "The study compared two instructions during a free-weight bench press: reach a target velocity of 1.0 m/s, or move as fast as possible. Thirteen male powerlifters performed 4 sets of 5 repetitions at 45% 1RM under each instruction, and their repetitions to failure at 75% 1RM were then compared. The target-velocity instruction produced a faster best repetition per set, with no difference in the subsequent repetition test.",
  "tldr": "Telling powerlifters to reach a challenging 1.0 m/s target produced slightly faster best-repetition bar speeds than telling them to move as fast as possible. The faster speeds did not reduce how many repetitions they completed in a later 75% 1RM set.",
  "methods": "Thirteen male powerlifters (of 15 tested) completed two randomised sessions of 4 sets of 5 bench press repetitions at 45% 1RM, under either a 1.0 m/s target or move-as-fast-as-possible instruction, with feedback after each repetition from a linear position transducer. Mean velocity of each repetition was measured with a 3D motion capture system, and the fastest mean velocity per set was compared by a 2 x 4 repeated-measures ANOVA. The 75% 1RM repetition test was compared by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.",
  "findings": "The fastest mean velocity per set averaged 0.84 m/s with the target instruction and 0.82 m/s with the move-as-fast-as-possible instruction (p=0.0002). Eleven of 13 participants were faster under the target instruction, by about 0.03 m/s on average, and only one exceeded the 1.0 m/s target. Repetitions completed at 75% 1RM were 9.6 with the target instruction and 10.0 with the other instruction (p=0.43).",
  "limitations": "Small sample of 13 male powerlifters, one exercise, one relative load and one target velocity. Only the fastest repetition of each set was analysed, and the authors state that using all repetitions may have shown no significant difference. The fixed target was not individualised and was out of reach for most participants. Acute velocity was measured, not training adaptations. The PDF states a 2019 publication year, while the Crossref record gives 2021; the PDF year is used here.",
  "practicalImplications": "A challenging velocity target, even one most lifters did not reach, produced slightly faster best-repetition bar speeds during bench press sets at 45% 1RM than a move-as-fast-as-possible cue, without reducing repetitions in a later set in the same session. The authors suggest individualised targets may work better than one fixed target. Load-velocity estimates of 1RM taken under one cue may not transfer to the other.",
  "athleteDev": "Coaches who monitor bar speed can try a challenging velocity target during bench press training to elicit faster best-repetition velocity. The effect was small (0.02 m/s on average) and was measured within one session with powerlifters only.",
  "rtp": "The study did not include injured athletes or return-to-sport testing, so it cannot be used to set velocity targets or judge readiness during rehabilitation or return to play."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary/findings/methods: described the 0.84 vs 0.82 m/s outcome as mean velocity across the sets -> it is the fastest mean velocity in each set ('The fastest mean velocity attained with a 45% 1RM load during each 5-repetition set was the dependent variable')",
   "screeningLimitations/limitations: added the authors' caveat that all-repetition averages may not differ ('if all repetitions in a set were considered ... there may have been no statistically significant differences')",
   "practicalImplications/athleteDev: 'attainable velocity target' -> the target was not attained by most ('One participant exceeded this 1.00 m/s target')",
   "citation: removed placeholder note and 00(00) issue string"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "PDF prints 2019 (online-first, 'J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2019') while crossrefYear is 2021, probably the issue year. PDF year kept per rules; reviewer should confirm.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q12",
 "sourceFile": "Effects of four different velocity-based training programming models on strength gains and physical performance.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Effects of Four Different Velocity-Based Training Programming Models on Strength Gains and Physical Performance' by Riscart-López et al. matches the filename and the Crossref title for externalDoi 10.1519/jsc.0000000000003934.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Randomised comparison of four 8-week velocity-based back squat programmes (linear, undulating, reverse and constant) in 43 young, moderately strength-trained men (physically active sport science students, 1.5 to 4 years of resistance training experience) who trained twice a week. All four groups increased 1RM squat, squat velocity, countermovement jump height and 20 m sprint performance within the group (for example, 1RM gains of 10.9% to 18.0%), but the authors report no significant group by time interactions for any outcome.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The sample was young, moderately strength-trained men who were physically active sport science students, not described as competitive athletes, and the study used a Smith machine and only two sessions a week. There was no non-training control group, and the constant group trained at a higher mean relative intensity than the others, so the study shows no detectable difference between models rather than a ranking of them.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the within-group gains as proof that a given velocity-based programme works, when the study found no significant between-model differences and had no untrained control group.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "Riscart-López J, Rendeiro-Pinho G, Mil-Homens P, Soares-daCosta R, Loturco I, Pareja-Blanco F, et al. Effects of four different velocity-based training programming models on strength gains and physical performance. J Strength Cond Res. 2020.",
  "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000003934",
  "abstract": "Forty-three moderately strength-trained men were randomly assigned to linear, undulating, reverse or constant velocity-based training models and followed an 8-week full squat programme. The authors report that all groups trained at similar average relative intensity, velocity loss, number of sets and rest. All groups improved 1RM, velocity-related outcomes, countermovement jump and 20 m sprint time, with no significant group by time interactions.",
  "tldr": "Four different velocity-based squat programming models, with 20% velocity loss, 3 sets and 4 minutes of rest, produced similar gains in squat strength, jump height and sprint time in moderately trained men over 8 weeks. The time course of strength gains looked less pronounced in the undulating group, but no between-group difference was statistically significant.",
  "methods": "Forty-six men were matched on 1RM and randomly assigned, and 43 completed an 8-week intervention of two sessions per week (linear n=11, undulating n=10, reverse n=11, constant n=11). Velocity was measured for every repetition with a linear velocity transducer, and loads were adjusted daily to the velocity-predicted %1RM. Pre- and post-tests included predicted 1RM, velocity at common loads, countermovement jump and 20 m sprint time, analysed with a 4 x 2 ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests.",
  "findings": "No significant group by time interactions were found for 1RM (p=0.18), velocity variables, countermovement jump (p=0.22) or sprint time (p=0.98). Within groups, 1RM rose significantly in all four groups (10.9% undulating to 18.0% reverse), with effect sizes of about 0.3 to 0.5 for jump height and 0.3 for sprint time. The constant group trained with a significantly slower average velocity and a higher mean relative intensity (about 67.5% vs 62.5% 1RM) than the other groups.",
  "limitations": "Smith machine used for testing and training, which limits transfer to free-weight training. Sample was moderately trained recreational men (not elite athletes), training frequency was two sessions a week, and there was no non-training control group. The abstract states all groups trained with similar relative average intensity, but Table 2 shows the constant group trained at a higher mean relative intensity (p<0.001) and the undulating group did fewer repetitions per set at 50% 1RM. The PDF prints 2020 as the publication year, while the Crossref record gives 2021; the PDF year is used here.",
  "practicalImplications": "In moderately trained men, a velocity-based squat programme using 20% velocity loss within sets, 3 sets and 4 minutes of rest produced similar strength and jump gains whichever loading model was used. Coaches can choose among these models for variety; the authors' observation that strength rose more slowly with undulating programming was not statistically significant and should not drive model choice on its own.",
  "athleteDev": "Velocity-based squat programming with monitored velocity loss was followed by gains in strength and jump performance in moderately trained adults, though without a control group. The four programming models gave similar results, so selection can rest on the coach's preference or the timing of the training block.",
  "rtp": "The study did not include injured people or a return-to-sport outcome. It cannot be used to set loads or progressions during rehabilitation or to judge readiness to return to play."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "limitations: added the abstract vs Table 2 conflict ('All groups trained with similar relative average intensity (67.5% 1RM)' vs 'The CP group trained with higher MRI-MPV than the other groups (CP: 0.88 ... [~67.5% 1RM] vs. LP: 0.96 ... [~62.5% 1RM]')",
   "findings: 'constant group trained with slower average velocity' -> also higher mean relative intensity; added interaction p-values",
   "screeningLimitations: 'groups differed in training intensity and loading patterns' -> stated the specific difference and the lack of a control group",
   "practicalImplications: 'which matters if strength gain is the priority' -> removed advice built on a non-significant observation ('no statistically significant differences between groups were found in the evolution of the estimated 1RM')",
   "athleteDev: causal wording softened because there was no control group",
   "citation: removed placeholder note"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "PDF prints 2020 (online-first, 'XX(X): 000-000, 2020') while crossrefYear is 2021. Figure 1 legend gives n=46 with 12 per group in three groups, while all other results use n=43.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q13",
 "sourceFile": "Effects of low load resistance training with vascular     occlusion on the mechanical properties of muscle and tendon.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Effects of Low-Load Resistance Training With Vascular Occlusion on the Mechanical Properties of Muscle and Tendon' by Kubo et al. matches the filename and the Crossref title for externalDoi 10.1123/jab.22.2.112.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Rehabilitation", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Within-subject study in nine healthy young men (age 25 years) who trained one knee extensor with low load (20% 1RM) and vascular occlusion, and the other with high load (80% 1RM) without occlusion, three times a week for 12 weeks. Both protocols increased maximal isometric torque and quadriceps muscle volume. Within each leg, only high-load training significantly increased vastus lateralis specific tension (5.5%), voluntary activation and tendon-aponeurosis stiffness (45.6 to 59.3 N/mm), but the direct comparisons between protocols were not statistically significant.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only nine men were studied, the design compared two legs in each person over one exercise, and no sport or performance task was measured. The between-protocol differences in strength gain (p=0.107) and stiffness gain (p=0.131) were not statistically significant, so the contrast rests on within-leg changes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the tendon result as showing that occlusion training fails to adapt tendon or that high-load training is needed for tendon health, when the direct comparison between protocols was not significant and only nine healthy men were studied.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2006,
  "citation": "Kubo K, Komuro T, Ishiguro N, Tsunoda N, Sato Y, Ishii N, et al. Effects of low-load resistance training with vascular occlusion on the mechanical properties of muscle and tendon. Journal of Applied Biomechanics. 2006;22:112-119.",
  "doi": "10.1123/jab.22.2.112",
  "abstract": "Nine participants trained one knee extensor with low load (20% of 1RM) and vascular occlusion and the other with high load (80% of 1RM) for 12 weeks, three days a week. Both protocols increased maximal isometric torque and muscle volume. Specific tension of the vastus lateralis and tendon-aponeurosis stiffness increased after high-load training but did not change after low-load occlusion training.",
  "tldr": "Low-load training with vascular occlusion increased knee extensor strength and muscle volume in healthy young men, but unlike high-load training it did not significantly raise muscle specific tension, voluntary activation or tendon stiffness within the trained leg. Direct comparisons between the two methods were not significant, so the difference is suggestive rather than shown.",
  "methods": "Nine healthy young men completed 12 weeks of unilateral knee extension, with each leg randomly assigned to low load (20% 1RM, 4 sets averaging 17.5 repetitions, 30 s rest, occlusion pressure raised every four weeks) or high load (80% 1RM, 4 sets of 10, 1 min rest). Outcomes were maximal isometric torque, muscle volume by 0.5 T MRI, voluntary activation by twitch interpolation, EMG, vastus lateralis specific tension, and tendon-aponeurosis and patella tendon stiffness by ultrasound. Data were analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA.",
  "findings": "Maximal torque rose 7.8% with low-load occlusion training and 16.8% with high-load training, and quadriceps volume rose in both (reported as 5.9% and 7.4%, p=0.195 between protocols). Voluntary activation (3.2%), mEMG (20.5%), specific tension (5.5%) and tendon-aponeurosis stiffness (45.6 to 59.3 N/mm) rose only after high-load training. Patella tendon stiffness and cross-sectional area did not change with either protocol, and between-protocol differences in torque gain (p=0.107) and stiffness gain (p=0.131) were not significant.",
  "limitations": "Only nine men were studied with one exercise and one 12-week programme, and both protocols were done in the same participants. Patella tendon elongation was not corrected for joint rotation, and specific tension used fascicle length during contraction rather than optimal length. The text reports muscle volume gains of 5.9% (low load) and 7.4% (high load), but Table 1 means (1892 to 2032 and 1878 to 2011 cm3) imply about 7.4% and 7.1%. The authors' suggestions that occlusion training could raise tendon injury risk or favour stretch-shortening performance were speculation and not tested.",
  "practicalImplications": "In healthy young men, 12 weeks of low-load training with vascular occlusion increased strength and muscle volume, but significant changes in tendon stiffness, voluntary activation and specific tension were seen only after high-load training. Coaches who use occlusion training to build size and strength should not assume it reproduces the tendon and neural adaptations of heavy loading.",
  "athleteDev": "This study gives mechanistic evidence that high-load training raised tendon stiffness, voluntary activation and specific tension while low-load occlusion training did not change them significantly. Because the between-protocol tests were not significant, it supports caution rather than a firm conclusion when tendon stiffness is a training goal.",
  "rtp": "The study used healthy men and did not test injured tendons or any return-to-sport outcome. It cannot show that low-load occlusion training is safe or effective for rehabilitating a tendon, so it should not be used to set return-to-play timelines."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary/tldr/athleteDev: within-leg significance was presented as a difference between methods ('appear to adapt the muscle-tendon unit differently') -> stated that between-protocol tests were not significant ('tended to be greater for HL than for LLO (p = 0.131)')",
   "screeningLimitations: 'only borderline (p=0.107 and p=0.131)' -> not statistically significant; removed muddled statement about uncorrected tendon outcome (only patella tendon elongation was uncorrected: 'we did not correct for the measurement of patella tendon elongation')",
   "findings: added voluntary activation and mEMG results that underpin the authors' conclusion ('increased significantly, 3.2% for HL (p = 0.031), but not for LLO'); consolidated to 3 sentences",
   "limitations: added text vs Table 1 conflict on muscle volume change (text 5.9% LLO; table 1892 to 2032 cm3)",
   "populations: Mixed / Unspecified -> Adult / Recreational (healthy non-athlete young men)"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "",
  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

input.content:
{
 "id": "Q14",
 "sourceFile": "Effects of Nightly Electronic Device Restriction and Morning Bright Light on Sleep, Mood, and Performance Among Elite Athletes (1).pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Effects of Nightly Electronic Device Restriction and Morning Bright Light on Sleep, Mood, and Performance Among Elite Athletes' by Hoshikawa matches the filename (a '(1)' download suffix only) and the Crossref title for externalDoi 10.1519/jsc.0000000000005201.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Athlete Wellbeing", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Randomised controlled trial of 25 elite athletes from 12 individual sports (12 in the intervention group, 13 in the control group) over 2 weeks. The intervention group turned off devices 30 minutes before bed and had 20 minutes of morning bright light (about 10,000 lux). Group by day interactions were significant for POMS vigor, reaction time, rebound jump height and rebound jump index, all of which improved within the intervention group, while actigraphy sleep measures did not change and the Epworth sleepiness and squat jump interactions were not significant (p=0.095 and p=0.085).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 25 athletes were analysed after 13 of the 38 randomised were excluded, leaving 12 and 13 per group, and the author reports a post hoc power of 0.68. The intervention group started with lower rebound jump height and index than controls, no blinding is described, and training could not be controlled.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as proof that screen restriction and morning light improve athletes' sleep or performance, when measured sleep did not change, the jump gains came in a group that started lower than controls, and comparisons were small and underpowered.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Hoshikawa M. Effects of nightly electronic device restriction and morning bright light on sleep, mood, and performance among elite athletes. J Strength Cond Res. 2025;39(11):1155-1162.",
  "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000005201",
  "abstract": "Twenty-five elite athletes were divided into an intervention group (n=12), who turned off electronic devices 30 minutes before bed and had 20 minutes of morning bright light (about 10,000 lux), and a control group (n=13). Sleep, sleepiness, mood and performance were monitored over 2 weeks. The intervention group improved POMS vigor, reaction time, rebound jump height and rebound jump index without a change in sleep parameters. Epworth sleepiness and squat jump changes were not significant between groups.",
  "tldr": "Two weeks of stopping device use 30 minutes before bed and 20 minutes of morning bright light was followed by better mood, reaction time and rebound jump performance in elite athletes compared with controls. Sleep did not change, and the sample was small with baseline differences in jump performance.",
  "methods": "Randomised controlled trial in 25 elite athletes (24 international, 11 men, 14 women) from 12 sports, allocated to intervention (n=12) or control (n=13), after 13 of 38 initially randomised athletes were excluded for pain, injury, illness or schedule reasons. Over 2 weeks, actigraphy, Karolinska sleepiness, subjective sleep quality, fatigue and morning heart rate were recorded daily. Before and after, Epworth sleepiness, POMS, psychomotor vigilance reaction time, grip strength, squat and rebound jumps, and exercise heart rate were measured and analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.",

{
 "id": "Q15",
 "sourceFile": "Effects of photobiomodulation on pain and return to play of injured athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Effects of Photobiomodulation on Pain and Return to Play of Injured Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis' by Morgan et al. matches the filename and the Crossref title for externalDoi 10.1519/jsc.0000000000004752.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Rehabilitation", "Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review of six randomised controlled trials (205 competitive and recreational athletes, mean age 24 years) of photobiomodulation for injury, with comparators of placebo, an aloe-based gel or standard physical therapy. Five trials reported pain and were pooled in a random-effects meta-analysis, which favoured photobiomodulation (SMD 1.03, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.63, p=0.0089, I2 46.9%). The two trials that measured return to play were summarised narratively and did not show a benefit.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only five small trials were pooled for pain, against a mix of placebo, aloe-based gel and standard physical therapy comparators, with moderate heterogeneity. The two return-to-play trials used different designs and could not be pooled. The protocol was not prospectively registered, and injury severity was not reported in the included studies.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the pooled pain effect as evidence that photobiomodulation shortens return to play, when the two trials that measured return to play did not show a benefit.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Morgan RM, Wheeler TD, Poolman MA, Haugen ENJ, LeMire SD, Fitzgerald JS. Effects of photobiomodulation on pain and return to play of injured athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(6):e310-e319.",
  "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000004752",
  "abstract": "This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated photobiomodulation (PBM) for musculoskeletal pain and time to return to play in injured athletes. Six randomised controlled trials, including 205 competitive and recreational athletes with a mean age of 24 years, were included. PBM reduced pain compared with control groups (SMD 1.03, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.63, p=0.0089). The two trials on time to return to play did not support a benefit of PBM.",
  "tldr": "In injured athletes, photobiomodulation reduced pain more than control treatments across five small randomised trials. The two trials that measured return to play did not show a benefit, so the pain result should not be read as proof that PBM speeds return to play.",
  "methods": "Systematic search of MEDLINE Complete, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, PubMed, Web of Science and Embase, with secondary searches to 7 November 2023, supplemented by reference lists and Google Scholar. Included studies were English-language peer-reviewed randomised controlled trials in athletes aged 18 to 44 years reporting pain or return to play after injury, screened independently by two reviewers with a third resolving disagreements. Quality was rated with the PEDro scale (Cohen's kappa 1), pain effects were pooled with a random-effects model in Meta-Essentials, and return-to-play data were summarised narratively.",
  "findings": "Six trials published between 2004 and 2022 were included, with PEDro scores of 6 to 10; five contributed pain data, and the pooled pain effect favoured photobiomodulation (SMD 1.03, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.63, p=0.0089, I2 46.9%). Of the two return-to-play trials, one found a shorter return with an aloe-based gel than with photobiomodulation (about 8 vs 11 days), and the other found no difference between photobiomodulation and placebo (about 23 to 24 days in each group).",
  "limitations": "The Abstract and Results say six RCTs were analysed, but only five trials measured pain (the sixth, Medeiros et al., measured return to play) and the Discussion and Limitations state the meta-analysis had five studies. The aloe comparator gel also contained arnica, devil's claw and tocopherol, and the hamstring trial was powered only for large effects. Heterogeneity was moderate, the protocol was not registered, injury severity was not reported, and small samples limit precision.",
  "practicalImplications": "Clinicians working with injured athletes may use photobiomodulation as an adjunct to reduce pain, with devices of 810 to 980 nm as in the included trials. The authors suggest 3 to 10 minutes per application, 3 to 4 times per week, for at least 3 to 8 weeks, but this dosing was not tested in the meta-analysis. It should not be expected to shorten time to return to play.",
  "athleteDev": "This review does not assess performance outcomes in healthy athletes, so it does not support photobiomodulation as a way to improve training or competition performance. Its findings apply to pain management in injured athletes.",
  "rtp": "The pain findings can inform symptom management during rehabilitation. The two return-to-play trials, with different comparators and no pooled estimate, showed no clear benefit, so the review cannot be used to set or shorten return-to-play timelines."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary/tldr/findings: implied six trials were pooled for pain -> five pooled ('Our meta-analysis of musculoskeletal pain only had 5 studies'; the Results sentence 'Six studies evaluated pain' cites only refs 3, 50, 52, 53, 57)",
   "limitations: resolved the 5 vs 6 inconsistency and added comparator and power caveats ('The aloe gel used in this study was not solely aloe vera'; 'this study was powered to detect large effects')",
   "practicalImplications: noted that the dosing advice is the authors' suggestion, not a tested result"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "The reported 95% CI (0.43 to 1.63) with SE 0.22 is consistent with a t-based interval on 4 degrees of freedom, supporting five pooled studies. In one pooled trial (Ammendolia) the gel comparator reduced pain more than PBM, so the direction of that study's SMD should be checked on the forest plot, which is not in the extracted text. Return-to-play content.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

  "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000004752",
  "abstract": "This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated photobiomodulation (PBM) for musculoskeletal pain and time to return to play in injured athletes.  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat a passed heat tolerance test as clearance that rules out recurrence, when the only recurrent heat stroke in the cited IDF data occurred in an athlete classified as heat tolerant and the criteria were developed for young soldiers.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "O'Connor FG, Heled Y, Deuster PA. Exertional heat stroke, the return to play decision, and the role of heat tolerance testing: a clinician's dilemma. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2018;17(7):244-248.",
  "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000000502",
  "abstract": "Exertional heat stroke is a leading preventable cause of morbidity and mortality in athletes and warfighters. Because a prior event is an important risk factor, return to play or duty decisions after heat stroke are difficult. This special communication reviews current guidance and evidence on these decisions and the potential role of heat tolerance testing, which exposes a person to a controlled heat load to assess heat tolerance.",
  "tldr": "Return to play after exertional heat stroke has no evidence-based guideline. The authors suggest combining history, clinical biomarkers and, where indicated, a heat tolerance test, which has useful but limited diagnostic data.",
  "methods": "Special communication. A clinical case is used to frame the problem. The authors review ACSM return-to-play recommendations, US and French military recurrence studies, and the Israel Defense Force heat tolerance test protocol and results. No systematic search is described.",
  "findings": "ACSM guidance is summarised as at least 7 days without exercise after release, follow-up tests at about 1 week, a gradual 2-week return in a cool environment, and a laboratory heat tolerance test if vigorous activity is not reached within 4 weeks; in a large US Army cohort, a prior serious heat illness was associated with 4.02 times the odds of a later mild event. In an IDF study, 6 of 145 soldiers tested after heat stroke had a recurrent heat illness (4 of 35 classified heat intolerant, 2 of 110 heat tolerant), only one of which was heat stroke and occurred in a heat-tolerant soldier, giving reported sensitivity, specificity and accuracy of 66.7%, 77.7% and 77.2%.   "limitations": "Selective narrative with no systematic search or quality appraisal, and the authors state their conclusions are a collective opinion. The HTT criteria come from young, moderately fit soldiers and are not adjusted for sex, aerobic capacity, training, acclimatisation or body fat. The recurrence and accuracy data come from a single military population and describe heat illness mostly as heat exhaustion, not heat stroke. The PDF prints 2018, matching Crossref.",
  "practicalImplications": "After exertional heat stroke, ACSM guidance as summarised here is to rest at least 7 days, recheck affected organs at about 1 week, and return gradually over about 2 weeks in a cool environment.   "athleteDev": "The article does not address performance training. Its heat tolerance test criteria were set for young, moderately fit soldiers and are not adjusted for fitness or acclimatisation, so it gives no guidance on heat training for healthy athletes.",
  "rtp": "This article is directly about return-to-play decisions after exertional heat stroke. It supports gradual reintroduction with follow-up testing, and the authors regard a successful heat tolerance test as a reliable tool when used within a broader decision process, while stating that data are insufficient to support it as a stand-alone diagnostic test and that no evidence-based guideline exists."
 },

  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Article is labelled a special communication and ends with a stated 'collective opinion'.   "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

content.text:
All eight records are in `verified/`, and they all pass the checker I wrote at `helpers/v02/validate.py`. That checker confirms valid JSON, only taxonomy values, the external DOI with `doiMissing` set to false, no em dashes, no placeholder citation strings, and the verification block. All eight are INCLUDE.

- **Q09**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. Only two of the three CBD studies were placebo-controlled; the first compared CBD with an MCT carrier oil and no treatment. The draft also missed the second recovery result, lower CK and myoglobin, and misreported the rugby survey (133 of 517 players had used CBD). The year 2022 is inferred because no year is printed in this accepted manuscript.
- **Q10**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The 0.84 vs 0.82 m/s result is the fastest repetition in each set, not the average of all repetitions, and the authors say the average might show no difference. The PDF prints 2019 but Crossref gives 2021.
- **Q11**: INCLUDE, DECISION_CHANGED (was EXCLUDE for relevance), high. This is a survey of how practitioners prescribe and screen for blood flow restriction training in injury rehabilitation: 83.4% use it for rehab and 21.4% work mainly in sport, so it is relevant to athlete health. The PDF prints 2023 but Crossref gives 2024. A reviewer should confirm the library wants this kind of survey.
- **Q12**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The abstract says all groups trained at the same average intensity, but Table 2 shows the constant group trained heavier (about 67.5% vs 62.5% 1RM). I also removed advice that rested on a non-significant trend. The PDF prints 2020 but Crossref gives 2021.
- **Q13**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, normal. The draft treated within-leg changes as a difference between the two methods; the direct comparisons were not significant (p=0.107 and 0.131). The muscle-volume percentages in the text do not match the Table 1 means.
- **Q14**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, normal. The abstract and table give different p-values for reaction time (0.016 vs 0.001). The intervention group started with lower jump scores, and some gains appeared in both groups.
- **Q15**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. Six trials were included but only five were pooled for pain; the draft implied all six. In one of the pooled trials the gel comparator reduced pain more than the laser, so someone should check the forest plot, which is not in the extracted text.
- **Q16**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high. The draft understated the authors' view of the heat tolerance test: they call it reliable within a wider decision but not as a stand-alone diagnostic. The only repeat heat stroke in the cited data happened in a soldier who had passed the test. The article is labelled a "special communication", so a reviewer may classify it as commentary rather than a review.
